guide.title: Norwich, Connecticut: Mill Town at the Head of the Thames
guide.intro: Norwich was established in 1658-59, when 69 families from Saybrook settled at the head of the Thames River in southeastern Connecticut. By 1694 residents had built a public landing there for trade, and through the nineteenth century the city grew into a manufacturing hub, producing textiles, armaments, and specialty goods along a rail line to Springfield. Smith & Wesson got its start here in 1852, developing the "Volcanic" repeating rifle at the water-powered confluence of the Shetucket and Yantic Rivers. Norwich is also the birthplace of Benedict Arnold, born in 1741 before his 1781 betrayal led him to burn nearby New London. Long before any of that, the gorge and waterfall at Uncas Leap on the Yantic River had already been sacred Mohegan ground since 1643, site of the Battle of Great Plains; the city acquired it as a heritage park in 2010. The 1675 Leffingwell House, once a Revolutionary-era tavern, still stands downtown.

sections.heading: Mill town at the head of the Thames
sections.body: Norwich was established in 1658-59, when 69 families from Saybrook settled at the head of the Thames River in southeastern Connecticut. By 1694 residents had built a public landing there for trade, and through the nineteenth century the city grew into a manufacturing hub, producing textiles, armaments, and specialty goods along a rail line to Springfield. Smith & Wesson got its start here in 1852, developing the "Volcanic" repeating rifle at the water-powered confluence of the Shetucket and Yantic Rivers. Norwich is also the birthplace of Benedict Arnold, born in 1741 before his 1781 betrayal led him to burn nearby New London. Long before any of that, the gorge and waterfall at Uncas Leap on the Yantic River had already been sacred Mohegan ground since 1643, site of the Battle of Great Plains; the city acquired it as a heritage park in 2010.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Norwich is a drive-to destination reached via I-395, connecting to CT Route 2/2A and Route 32, with routes from Boston, Hartford, New York, and Providence all converging there. There is no rail station in Norwich itself — the nearest trains are at New London Union Station to the south, the terminus of Shore Line East commuter rail and also an Amtrak Northeast Corridor stop.

sections.heading: Museums, a playhouse, and a Georgian-manor spa
sections.body: The Slater Memorial Museum, on the Norwich Free Academy campus, is one of only two museums in the country situated on a high school campus, holding roughly 10,000 objects by about 1,000 artists. The 1675 Leffingwell House, a pre-Revolutionary tavern by 1701, opens seasonally April through October. Chestnut Street Playhouse stages community theater year-round downtown. For an overnight stay, The Spa at Norwich Inn occupies a 1929 Georgian-manor estate on 42 acres, now owned by the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation, with 27 treatment rooms and two on-site restaurants.

faq.question: How do I get to Norwich?
faq.answer: Norwich is reached via I-395, connecting to CT Route 2/2A and Route 32. There is no rail station in Norwich — the nearest is New London Union Station to the south, served by Shore Line East and Amtrak's Northeast Corridor.

faq.question: What is Uncas Leap Heritage Park?
faq.answer: A 1.2-acre city park on the Yantic River featuring a gorge and waterfall that has been sacred Mohegan ground since 1643, marking where the Battle of Great Plains between the Mohegan and Narragansett Tribes concluded. The city acquired the site in 2010.

faq.question: What is the Slater Memorial Museum?
faq.answer: A museum on the Norwich Free Academy campus, one of only two museums in the country situated on a high school campus, with roughly 10,000 objects by about 1,000 artists from five continents. Open Monday, Wednesday-Saturday, 10 a.m.-4 p.m.

faq.question: Was Benedict Arnold from Norwich?
faq.answer: Yes — Arnold was born in Norwich in 1741. Forty years later, on September 6, 1781, he led the British burning of nearby New London before fleeing to England, where he died in 1801.

faq.question: What is The Spa at Norwich Inn?
faq.answer: A destination spa resort on a 1929 Georgian-manor estate, now owned by the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation, with 27 treatment rooms, pools, and two on-site restaurants.

places.name: Slater Memorial Museum
places.summary: Located on the Norwich Free Academy campus, it is one of only two museums in the country situated on a high school campus and holds roughly 10,000 objects by about 1,000 artists from five continents, operating for more than a century. Open Monday, Wednesday-Saturday, 10 a.m.-4 p.m.

photos.description: The exterior of the Slater Memorial Museum on the Norwich Free Academy campus.
photos.author: Mark Landon

places.name: Leffingwell House Museum
places.summary: A 1675 two-room home that became a pre-Revolutionary tavern by 1701 and by 1776 was the townhouse of Patriot Christopher Leffingwell; the adjacent Joseph Carpenter Silversmith Shop is also toured. Open seasonally April-October, Saturdays 11 a.m.-3 p.m. ($8/person); tours by appointment year-round.

places.name: Uncas Leap Heritage Park
places.summary: A 1.2-acre city heritage site sacred to the Mohegan Tribe since 1643, featuring a gorge and waterfall on the Yantic River plus a nineteenth-century mill ruin; connected to the Walk Norwich trail system via the 2.8-mile Heritage Trail and roughly 1-mile Uncas Leap Trail. Open year-round with wheelchair-accessible water views.

places.name: Chestnut Street Playhouse
places.summary: A community theater in downtown Norwich staging musicals, plays, and cabaret events year-round.

places.name: Epicure Brewing
places.summary: An independent craft brewery and taproom in the historic Norwich Harbor district, with a regular live-music schedule.

places.name: Olde Tymes Restaurant
places.summary: A family-style local landmark serving classic home cooking — breakfast, lunch, and dinner — for over 42 years.

places.name: The Spa at Norwich Inn
places.summary: A 1929 Georgian-manor estate on 42 acres — inn rooms date to its 1930 opening — now a destination spa resort owned by the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation, with 27 treatment rooms, pools, Kensington's Restaurant, and Ascot's Pub.
